newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila c. bank to sell dlr forwards to banks - BAP.
newsitem.headline: Manila c. bank to sell dlr forwards to banks - BAP.

text.p: The Philippine central bank is set to sell dollar forward contracts to onshore banks to ease the pressure on the peso, Bankers Association of the Philippines (BAP) president Deogracias Vistan said on Monday.
He said central bank has agreed in principle to issue 30-day renewable forward dollars to banks which have open Non-Deliverable Forwards (NDF) positions.
The central bank last week suspended the sale of dollar NDF by onshore banks to offshore banks.

"They will be given 30-day renewable forwards so that they will not add to the demand in the spot market. These are renewable at the option of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (central bank)," he told reporters after meeting other bank presidents.
"We just isolated the demand sources for spot dollars," he added.
He said the central bank will also sell dollar forwards to onshore foreign banks which have large dollar demand.
"A number of foreign banks which may have large invisible requirements will be given up to 90-day forward contracts. This is not renewable," Vistan said.
Vistan said foreign banks were singled out in the second forward contracts because they have access to dollars from their head offices.
"This will allow them to be able to sell their own dollars which will help the system," he said.
Foreign banks have been requested to stay away from the spot market, he added.
"This is the time when they need to show what it is they're here in the Philippines for."

The peso has been wobbly since the de fact devaluation 17 days ago. Speculation in other regional currencies still put pressure on the peso, forcing the central bank to defend the peso albeit in a more limited scale.
"We've got to send a very, very strong signal to dollar holders, which are the exporters and dollar depositors, that rates could come down and they had better unload," Vistan said.

"We want to promote a stable foreign exchange rate. We think the NDF and foreign banks' spot cash requirements are two pressure points. All the BAP has done is to suggest a way where those two pressure points can be put aside and let the more normal type of purchases in the market reflect the true requirements," Vistan added.
